HUNGARY – Careful and patient NBH amid a positive credit risk cycle The positive mood on Hungarian assets post-election remains, further supported by the positive policy signalling on the announcement of plans for Euro adoption by 2031. Nonetheless, there remains unanswered questions about the direction of post-election fiscal policy. It’s unclear how seriously we should take the 40-page Tisza campaign document signalling a mix of costly expenditure policies, which are likely a function of having to accommodate disparate interests of party coalition members. There is expectation that household benefits provided by the previous Fidesz government will be maintained, and that personal income tax system is likely to become more progressive, incorporating some wealth tax element. With the new government inheriting significant pre-election fiscal slippages, they could take two approaches at the onset of their government— either: 1) deliver campaign promises and blame the previous government for fiscal slippage; or, 2) focus on Euro criteria and pursue serious fiscal consolidation. A key date to watch is the 4th of May when parliament appoints the Prime Minister, though it’s not clear if key cabinet appointments will also be made in the same day. Asia Credit: high exposure to the energy shock The backdrop for APAC credit remains one of elevated uncertainty, with Asia seen as most exposed to the energy shock. The critical issue for credit agencies across the region is the evaluation of policy responses, especially on subsidies, tax measures and fertilizer price support schemes. There was also a lot of commentary how the changing geopolitics and US’s fiscal dynamics would undermine the US Treasury more structurally. As a means of diversification, investors favored EM across asset classes and were generally bullish commodities. In fact, we found that EM credit-focused investors have rotated heavily into EM local, with several reporting their highest local EM allocations in years. Within credit, investors favor high-yield idiosyncratic stories while exercising greater caution in African frontier markets, where the “easy” USD environment is ending and FX volatility is expected to rise in response to geopolitical uncertainties. We expect Latin America to capture a disproportionate share of new EM capital flows given more favorable energy security profiles and elevated real yields. On the risks side, only Iran really dominated the discussion. Private credit also was mentioned frequently, though most, including the IMF, downplayed it as a major macro risk, as deteriorating credit quality liquidity issues are seen as manageable, with contained impact on banks. A buyer strike in government bond markets was also discussed as a risk, partly because bonds sold off significantly during the Iran crisis. The overall mood was generally constructive as investors expect a relatively quick and favorable resolution of the war, with de-risking being replaced by wait and see. Experts suggest a deal is likely to come in the coming weeks, but most recent developments may warrant more caution. From de-risking to wait-and-see Even though uncertainty remains high regarding the final outcome of the war and the timing of its resolution, investors are increasingly comfortable looking through the mild stagflationary shock and adding risk where the stories are most resilient. The price action in the US stock market and selective LatAm stories reflects that mood. Europe is widely seen as the most impacted region within DM, and MENA and ASEAN within EM. If the energy shock remains contained, EM can benefit from renewed inflows. Within DM, on the one hand a quick resolution can benefit Europe as being the most vulnerable region. On the other hand, the K-shaped consumption dynamics has contributed to the resilience of the US economy to the energy shock so far. records.text: Similarities with the 2000s cycle US shale’s plateauing is reminiscent of the trajectory seen in traditional offshore basins in the late 1990s After 15 years of extraordinary growth, supplying 60% of the global non-OPEC supply increase, US shale oil is reaching maturity and is starting to plateau. In the late 1990s, as global spare capacity was running down and the oil market was simultaneously searching for new frontiers of growth, traditional offshore provinces such as Mexico, the Gulf of Mexico and the North Sea were already flattening out. Today, a similar dynamic is emerging with US shale ageing gracefully but still increasingly plateauing, particularly crude oil, and residual growth largely concentrated in NGLs. Looking at previous mature basins, UK production peaked in 1999, declining at a c.5% CAGR since then, Norway peaked in 2001 with a c.2% CAGR decline, Mexico peaked in 2004 with a c.3% decline, and the Gulf of Mexico peaked in 2002 with a 0.5% decline. Türkiye: Not immune but resilient The latest geopolitical shock and higher energy prices have worsened the outlook for inflation and the balance of payments, but the current policy framework appears well positioned to contain macro stability risks. Market revisions vary depending on oil and gas assumptions, but are meaningful: inflation is seen 3–5pp higher and the current account deficit 1–1.6% of GDP wider. We now see end 2026 inflation at 28.5% (from 24% pre war) and the current account deficit at US$60bn (3.4% of GDP), up from US$33bn (1.8%) pre war and pre data revisions. Reserves were hit hard by the unwinding of carry trades and portfolio outflows, but domestic confidence in FX stability held up, limiting retail dollarization. This likely reflects both the programme’s growing track record in absorbing shocks and the CBRT’s swift response early in the war, including raising the effective funding rate. Since the ceasefire announcement, carry inflows have resumed. Shared ownership creates shared price dynamics – and that co-movement, once stripped of common risk factors, is precisely what we seek to capture. Construction Methodology The construction proceeds in two steps. For each stock in our US momentum basket (BNPFMOM1 Index), we run a time-series regression of daily returns against the S&P 500 and four Dow Jones equity style factors: momentum, value, quality and low beta. These five regressors absorb the bulk of systematic return variation, namely market beta and factor exposures. What remains – the residual – is in theory idiosyncratic to each stock. We then compute the average pairwise correlation of these residuals across all holdings in the basket. This cross-sectional average becomes our crowding score, percentile-ranked against its own history to produce a 0–100 reading (Figure 3). The link to crowding is intuitive. Under normal conditions, idiosyncratic residuals should be largely uncorrelated – by construction, there is no common factor driving them. records.text: Australia Multi-Asset 20 April 2026 Citi Research 47 Insurance What is the likely impact of oil price inflation on insurers? A prolonged period of higher oil prices will likely have a flow on impact to claims costs (which are not necessarily correlated with CPI but can be) and potentially act as a headwind for the general insurance sector. At face value, rising fuel prices and geopolitical tensions leads to supply chain disruptions and additional inflationary pressure on home and motor claims. For example, higher construction materials costs or lengthier motor repair times could increase cost of claims. Commercial insurers are also not immune with NTI, a specialist transport/logistics insurer cautioning that “everything you buy is going to go up slightly – even if this was finished tomorrow, you’d have a three- to six-months supply chain issue before getting back to normal” . However, at this stage, it seems hard to conclude exactly the magnitude of the margin impact on insurers given the uncertainty with how long the fuel prices stay higher for longer and how quickly insurers can increase premiums. At present, it appears as if the share prices for Australian general insurance stocks are incorporating a relatively benign outlook for inflation and/or potentially allowing for the impact of inflation to be offset by both improved investment yield and stronger top line growth. records.text: M Update Morgan Stanley Research 3 drove a sequential deceleration in prices, with the 12-month rate slowing materially to 4.0% from 5.4%. The deceleration was driven almost entirely by restaurant prices, where inflation slowed sharply to 3.2%Y from 7.8%, reflecting the final unwind of GST/HST base effects. Restaurant prices alone subtracted 0.3pp from headline on the month, marking a clear reversal from prior months where they had been a key upside driver. In contrast, grocery inflation re-accelerated modestly, with food purchased from stores rising 4.4%Y, supported in part by higher prices for fresh vegetables. Energy prices were the clear driver of the upside surprise in March inflation. The shift in energy from -9.3%Y in February to +3.9%Y in March accounted for roughly 70bp of the increase in headline CPI, effectively explaining the entire re-acceleration in the annual rate. Within energy, the move was concentrated in gasoline. Prices rose sharply on the month, reflecting the supply shock associated with the Middle East conflict, and the pass-through to consumer prices appears high—consistent with prior episodes and our fiscal note assumptions. In contrast, other energy components remained relatively contained. Natural gas prices continued to decline on a year-over-year basis, and electricity prices showed only modest increases, limiting the breadth of the energy shock. The result is a narrow, gasoline-led energy impulse rather than a generalized energy inflation cycle.

Rather than seeing a “disconnect” between very cautious EM policymakers and relatively sanguine market participants, we think the latter is the endogenous byproduct of this precise vigilance. In other words, as EM CBs preserve policy buffers given worries about inflation tail risks, markets don’t need to worry as much about them. Moreover, some EM structural reforms have so far weathered the Iran shock with credibility intact, including using FX as a shock absorber in Egypt, or allowing more market- based fuel pricing in Nigeria, Sri Lanka or Pakistan, not to mention a post- election turnaround story in Hungary. Nonetheless, because the Iran conflict trajectory plays such a strong role in shaping macroeconomic outcomes, investor positioning in EM still looks well below the underlying bullish sentiment. INDONESIA – A Slightly Hawkish Central Bank Bias Prior to the Mideast crisis, we believe BI thought there was room to cut rates by up to 50bps. Growth was forecast to grow at 5.3% driven by household consumption, fiscal spending and loosening monetary policy, the latter justified by an output gap BI believed was still negative, with inflation remaining within the target band (2.8% on headline, core at 2.5%). However, the Middle East crisis has changed BI’s monetary policy strategy, and we think a rate hike is plausible on extended FX pressures, as we discussed in an earlier note. BI has already relinquished the option to cut another 50bps, holding policy rates at 4.75%, but signaled readiness to adjust policy rate if need. For now, we think it is pursuing a three-pronged approach amid global uncertainties: 1) FX intervention to stabilize the rupiah; 2) Support the economy through liquidity injection via government bond purchases and macro-prudential easing (e.g. reserve requirement cuts for priority lending); 3) Attract short-term portfolio flows/carry trades via increasing SRBI rates

records.text: The industry needs to replenish its pipeline of growth through exploration Following a decade of resource expansion that ended in 2017, our latest Top Projects edition shows an ongoing steepening of the oil cost curve. This is driven by project delays, capex and opex inflation, and higher taxes, as well as the increasing cost of capital for hydrocarbon projects. We estimate that the hurdle rate for giant long-cycle oil developments has risen from 10% in the 2004-14 cycle to 15+% in recent years. If we apply this higher cost of capital across the Top Projects cost curve, the marginal incentive price (the 75th percentile of the cost curve) is no longer $66/bbl, but $85/bbl (at 15% hurdle rates) and up to $115/bbl (at 20% hurdle rates). With exploration capex still c.60% below its peak and conventional discoveries at multi-decade lows, the cost curve has continued to steepen since 2017, with higher breakevens underscoring the need for a meaningful step-up in exploration spend to replenish the inventory of projects. As a result, we now expect an acceleration of deepwater FIDs from the supermajors, particularly across the Americas (Brazil, Gulf of America), West Africa (Nigeria, Angola) and new frontier basins such as Namibia. The fact that American navy ships have been able to go through the Strait during the Pakistan talks demonstrated to some that Iran was either unwilling or unable to keep it closed. On this view, the Strait will open shortly. This was not a consensus view. Central Banks generally still Cautious Our overall reading from various central banks was that uncertainty was just too high to commit to any strong reactions. Some central banks had not yet updated their forecasts post Iran shock, which makes it harder to lay out a flight plan. There was clear sense that the energy shock could be more concerning than the average supply shock, given the starting point of inflation and the recent central bank history with "transitory" inflation. Many central banks, including Brazil, certainly focus more on the inflationary part of the shock, rather than the negative growth aspect. Longer-term inflation expectations have not reacted much, giving central banks some time to wait and see. Even Japan, which had already been hawkish before the conflict, is suggesting both upside and downside risks to inflation from this shock, as the oil spike may undermine consumption, despite Japan having seen another robust wage round. For Australia, it was noted that give the strong initial conditions, the risk of pass through of inflation shocks is more elevated. Overall, caution was the name of the game in monetary policy. records.text: Australia Multi-Asset 20 April 2026 Citi Research 3 Key Takeaways Economics & Rates View Stagflation is the central risk, not just inflation. Australia faces potentially its worst stagflation episode since the 1970s. Year-average GDP has been downgraded from 2.5% to 2.0% in 2026, household consumption growth is cut to 1.6%, and headline CPI peaks at 5.5% YoY in Q2-26. The RBA must hike despite slowing growth, in our view; two 25bp hikes across May and June, taking the cash rate to 4.60%, with risks skewed toward more. The recession probability is assessed at 25%. We expect rate cuts likely to resume in 2027. Australia pays a premium on the Brent oil price. Australia faces a structurally higher effective oil cost compared to Brent oil because of its heavy reliance on Asian refiners, which are highly exposed to Strait of Hormuz supply chains. This systematically incorporates higher Singapore refining margins, Asian oil stack price premiums as well as incrementally higher freight and insurance costs. Historically, Australian imports have paid a premium to the spot oil prices. Generally, this premium has been low and manageable, particularly during times of stability. However, given the current crisis is not just a price shock but a physical supply shock, we believe the premium could be higher for Australian producers than historic averages. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear Intuition & Rationale The third indicator shifts the lens from price dynamics and options markets to fundamental valuation of the momentum basket. The premise is straightforward: if crowding creates excess capital in winners at losers' expense, it should leave a detectable imprint not only in prices and volatility surfaces but also in the relative valuation multiples of the long and short legs. Construction Methodology We construct it as follows. For each stock, we retrieve three valuation multiples – price-to-earnings (PE), price- to-sales (PS), and price-to-book (PB). We compute a weighted aggregate valuation for the long leg using positive exposures, and a similar measure for the short leg using absolute negative exposures. The spread is the log-ratio of short-to-long valuation, capturing how expensive the long leg trades relative to the short leg. We z-score this spread against its expanding history, interpreting the indicator relative to its own past distribution and avoiding look-ahead bias. The final composite valuation spread is the simple average of the three z-scores – PE, PS and PB – giving a more robust reading than any single multiple. A high z- score indicates the long leg trades at a historically elevated premium relative to the short leg, beyond normal cross-sectional valuation dispersion. Natural gas supply in Europe declined by about 20% between 2021 and 2023/24, and the consumption response was relatively evenly spread across industry, services and households (Exhibit 5, left). Oil consumption remained flat compared to 2021 levels. Our commodities team currently estimate a roughly 8% hit to global oil production in March, and a hit to Persian Gulf exports of about 12% of global oil supply. While about 20% of global LNG supply that typically passes through the Strait of Hormuz is currently blocked, LNG accounts for only about 15% of global gas supply and about 45% of EU gas supply, and the hit to EU gas supply would therefore be meaningfully lower than in 2022/23.2 Furthermore, our commodities analysts expect LNG supply to increase substantially over the coming years. 2 While our commodities analysts initially expected Europe having to deliver most of the demand response to the LNG supply shock, they recently noted that China reduced its net LNG demand notably, reducing the supply shock to Europe. Therefore, we still see the RBA cutting policy rates next year. Our view is for three 25bp cuts now back to 3.85% by Q3, with quarterly 25bp cut increments starting in February. We cannot rule out a sharp hiking cycle and then a reversal of rates a little earlier if growth is worse than expected and the unemployment rate jumps more than forecast. Rates Strategy view A brutal time to hold bonds… Aussie bonds have not been immune to the global bond sell-off since the start of the Middle East Crisis. Even so, the benchmark 10- year has underperformed the US, while the curve has bear-flattened materially. Our views on the 1y1y-5y5y flattening played out well. But this was fortuitous than anything else because of the Middle-East crisis. Working the other way, our view of front-end flattening did not play out for the same reason. But given still hawkish risks on the horizon, we continue to hold our pay May OIS trade which we had entered at attractive levels. Front-end pricing for another two hikes seems fair in our view. records.text: 2 Insights SPOTLIGHT VIEWS: TAKING A STANCE ON THE USD Time to go underweight the USD. This week we are adding a USD underweight to the portfolio for the first time since February. While the shifting finality of a ceasefire is the new status quo, the market is giving the powers at be the benefit of the doubt, or at the least looking through some of the risks of the conflict continuing. As such , our MKT MediaStats Narrative Map shows international conflict returning to “unimportant hype” for the USD. As the impetus for USD strength fades, there are signs the FX market is reverting back to its 2025 playbook of net selling. Real money investors have been net USD sellers since April 9th – even throughout conflicting headlines- with short term flows signalling selling momentum is just beginning to pick up steam. Transmission of data. As March economic data continue to flow through trader’s terminals, markets are increasingly able to refocus on the transmission of data into asset valuations. Since the start of April, G10 economic surprises have generally skewed weaker—either missing expectations outright or beating only marginally—across 8 of 10 countries. At the same time, monetary policy expectations for December 2026 have partially reversed. Simultaneously, inflation signals have remained hot at the headline level, though core measures appear more insulated for now, with some notable exceptions. April meeting preview: Our view is that the BCCh will stay on hold at its 28 April meeting. While the minutes of the prior meeting showed that several board members felt giving some thought to the option of a 25bp rate rise was reasonable, we interpret this not as forward guidance but rather as a sign that the BCCh considers the risks to be unbalanced. For the central bank, the risk that short-term inflation becomes more persistent currently outweighs the potential negative implications for growth of higher energy prices. However, we believe evidence on second- round effects is still insufficient to support raising the policy rate this month. records.text: Bloomberg FX: Expect USD/JPY to Consolidate Near the Highs Since tensions in the Middle East intensified at the end of February, risk assets have at times seen sharp declines, but the JPY has not performed particularly well. If Governor Ueda places greater weight on downside risks to growth than upside risks to underlying inflation, the initial market reaction could be toward JPY weakness. At present, our estimates of labor productivity do not point to labor replacement as the main source of faster productivity growth. In contrast, we find that its faster growth reflected faster output growth rather than slower employment growth ( Exhibit 3 ). And the acceleration in output growth was because of the industries with high-AI exposure; output growth slowed in the mid- and low-AI aggregates. Employment growth stagnated regardless of AI exposure, leaving employment trends across our three industry subgroups broadly similar. In AI Labor Disruption: More Micro Than Macro So Far, we had seen that "splitting industries by AI exposure yields no clear disruption signal: employment in more-exposed industries has not underperformed, and detrending/cyclical adjustments do not flip the story." Hence, faster labor productivity growth is presently more about changes in the numerator (output) in high-AI exposed sectors, than it is about changes in the denominator (employment).

E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 422/04/2026 Intuition & Rationale Our second indicator approaches crowding from a different angle entirely – not via the lens of realised price co-movement, but rather through what the options market is pricing into the momentum basket. The intuition is simple: when a trade is crowded, investors express growing conviction in its continuation through the options market. In turn, that directional consensus leaves a detectable imprint on the implied volatility surface. Construction Methodology For each stock in our US long/short momentum basket (BNPFMOM1 Index), we decompose the implied skewness of the return distribution into two distinct components. The upside skew is constructed as the spread between the three-month implied volatility at a 120% strike and the at-the-money (ATM) implied volatility, computed separately for the long and short legs of the factor and then weighted accordingly. A high reading signals pricing of strong continuation on the long leg in options, i.e. investors are expressing growing conviction that momentum winners will keep winning. The downside skew mirrors this logic: it compares the three- month implied volatility at an 80% strike to ATM, again across both legs. records.text: 2. Has the market already moved to price your baseline growth forecasts? Growth pricing already looks close to our baseline forecast for 1-year-ahead US GDP growth, though lower than our forecasts for growth beyond the next 2-3 quarters. Our usual benchmarking method suggests that the market is pricing US 1-year forward growth of around 1.9-2.0%, right around our current forecast for that horizon of 1.9% (Exhibit 4). Our preferred basket of US cyclical vs defensive stocks is also clearly back above its pre-war level, though not yet back to the February highs. Our growth and policy shock decompositions show too that the market has more than reversed the negative growth shock since the start of the war, while the hawkish policy shock has only partially reversed (Exhibit 5). Our medium-term growth outlook is a little stronger—around 2.2% through 2027—so to the extent that markets are willing to extend their horizon beyond any near-term slowdown from the oil shock and fading fiscal support, that deeper forward view may not yet be fully incorporated. But relative to the situation we described two weeks ago, where the market was putting meaningful weight on adverse scenarios (our growth pricing measure troughed around 1.1% on March 30), there has clearly been a sharp relaxation about growth risk already. The main theme in energy-exporting Kazakhstan is KZT appreciation supported by improving in both fundamentals and a policy framework. Kazakhstan: resilient growth with tighter policy KZT has appreciated by around 6% YTD, which is seen as broadly in line with fundamentals rather than a source of concern. The currency is not viewed as overvalued, despite 1Q seasonality, with support coming from high carry, sizeable inflows into local bonds, tighter domestic liquidity and strong oil prices. Foreign participation in the government securities market has roughly doubled over the past year, as tighter fiscal policy and FX borrowing by quasi sovereign entities (i.e. NIH “Baiterek”) have further supported the currency. The authorities also remain committed to the current FX selling policy to mirror gold purchases to smooth out KZT/FX flows and reduce pro cyclicality. The macro backdrop remains resilient, with robust non oil activity offsetting volatility in the energy sector. Oil production fell by around 20% in the first quarter, but growth elsewhere in the economy more than compensated, underscoring diversification progress. The result is a narrow, gasoline-led energy impulse rather than a generalized energy inflation cycle. Looking ahead, the near-term path for headline inflation is likely to be pushed higher by mechanical base effects and commodity price dynamics. The removal of the consumer carbon levy on April 1, 2025 will begin to drop out of the year-over-year comparison starting with the April print, which we estimate will add roughly 60bp to headline inflation. Combined with the recent increase in gasoline prices, this is likely to push headline inflation closer to 3% in April, even in the absence of further increases in spot energy prices. That said, the trajectory beyond the near term remains more balanced. Our commodity strategists expect North American natural gas prices to remain relatively benign and decoupled from global benchmarks, which should keep both natural gas and electricity inflation contained. As a result, the persistence of the energy shock will depend primarily on the path of oil prices. Under current assumptions for WCS/WTI and Henry Hub, we would expect headline inflation to peak in April–May before easing in subsequent months, although the outlook remains highly sensitive to further developments in energy markets. Third, the current shock is far less Europe-specific and more global in nature. In n 2022/23, energy market shifts were largely focused on Europe, leading to major cost disadvantages for energy-intensive industries, particularly relative to China, and a surge in import competition. This time, energy price pressures are more global, with Asia appearing to be affected to a similar (or even greater) extent. European energy-intensive industries therefore look less exposed to competitiveness pressures. Non-energy intensive industries—that previously substituted more expensive domestic energy-intensive intermediates with lower cost imports—are likely to be relatively more exposed to the current shock. Taken together, our analysis suggests that the overall impact of the current n energy price shock on European manufacturing should be notably smaller than in 2022, with the shock expected to be less severe and less persistent. A cap rate is essentially the ratio of a property's net operating income (NOI) to its market value. A lower cap rate generally implies a higher valuation for a given income stream, and vice-versa. Fluctuations in cap rates directly impact property valuations, and these movements are influenced by a myriad of factors, including interest rates, risk perception, market demand, and income growth prospects. Treasury yields moved lower Friday on the news that the Strait of Hormuz was fully open to commercial vessels. However, the current opening of the strait is unclear as we go to print Sunday. Regardless, Friday’s price action made it clear that WTI forwards contained a large term premium. Or in other words, oil prices will move lower by year-end, which reopens the path for further rate cuts to be priced in (Figure 4; see US Rates Weekly - Short-term uncertainty but long-term value). We have remained long Treasuries during the Middle East conflict based on our view that fair value has not moved from our YE26 forecast for 10y yields to go below 4%. The crux of our argument is that the forward curve is pricing in too few rate cuts, at slightly more than one, as presumably a Fed on hold in 2026 should justify sharper and deeper rate cuts in 2027 /2028. At the same time, a low-hire, low-fire economy opens a large downside yield asymmetry. The JOLTS data from two weeks ago reported the hiring rate reaching new local lows (see US Rates Weekly - Hedging our bullish lean into CPI). CEEMEA EGYPT: Flexible FX Policy Commended, Surprisingly Resilient Revenues The central bank remains committed to shift towards an inflation targeting framework and establish a more flexible FX regime. While some may have argued that the FX volatility on the back of the Iran crisis had been excessive, a key conclusion of Egypt’s experience is that currency flexibility worked in acting as a primary shock absorber. Despite significant depreciation driven by sizeable portfolio outflows (they estimate foreign portfolio flows have declined to about $25bn from a peak of $39bn), we did not see a parallel market emerge, and instead, local/domestic residents increased EGP purchases to counterbalance the market (rather than previous historical experience of locals amplifying FX shocks). CBE will likely proceed in a more “measured” pace of monetary easing as its disinflation trajectory has been “slightly disrupted” (+3.2% MoM/15.2% YoY in March). Inflation is no longer expected to be within the target band of 7±2% by year-end, shifting the timetable to 2H27. Authorities will likely need to grapple with domestic energy price adjustments, FX pass-thru effects and elevated global commodities. However, “deep positive real rates” provide them a buffer. Next up: AI and labor productivity In this report, we put another lesson from history to the test and examine whether AI usage is leading to faster productivity growth. We focus our analysis on labor productivity, using industry-level data on output and employment to construct industry-level output per worker. We also plan on using this analysis as an ongoing tracker of AI diffusion and productivity. Our main conclusions are as follows: Key takeaways: We find positive correlation between industry-level AI exposure and faster labor productivity growth. We estimate that industries with high AI exposure contributed 1.7pp of the 2.4pp growth in output per employee in the four quarters through 4Q 2025. Furthermore, its contribution accelerated: it contributed only 0.7pp in 2024. Faster productivity growth has been driven by faster output growth, as opposed to labor replacement. Trends in employment growth have been similar across industries with different AI exposure, while output growth has accelerated more rapidly in industries that Morgan Stanley Research has identified as higher AI exposure. Among industries with high AI exposure, the industries that rose fastest over the past year also tended to have accelerated the most, thereby accounting for the overall pickup in productivity. The tech industries led the way (Exhibit 7 ). And within them, it's again output strength rather than employment weakness that drives the productivity growth. The 60bp move in headline inflation was entirely explained by energy prices, while core and good inflation softened at the margin. records.text: Difference 3: The Current Shock is Less Concentrated on Europe Third, the energy price shock in 2022 was geographically asymmetric, while the current shock affects Asia to a similar (or even higher degree) compared to Europe. Broadly, energy prices in Europe increased by almost 200% between early 2021 and mid-2022, while energy prices in the US increased by less than 100% and energy prices in China by about 10% (Exhibit 7, left). European energy prices remained about 75% above their pre-crisis levels throughout 2023 and 2024, while they remained only about 25% higher in the US and only about 10% higher in China. This asymmetric energy price shock translated into substantial cost disadvantages for energy-intensive industries in Europe, in particular relative to China. The increase in European producer prices relative to China was much higher in energy-intensive than in non-energy intensive industries (Exhibit 7, right). records.text: asons. In the context of equity factors, it manifests as an excess accumulation of capital in stocks that score highly on a particular characteristic. The mechanism is self- reinforcing: as a factor attracts inflows, its constituent stocks are bid upward, performance improves, further inflows follow and the pattern resumes. The trade becomes consensus, and consensus trades are fragile. The risk is not merely theoretical. When positioning gets sufficiently crowded, even a modest shift in sentiment can trigger a disorderly unwind. The August 2007 “quant crisis” remains the canonical episode, but the momentum crashes of early 2009 and late 2018 share the same fingerprints, as does 2021’s post-Covid reflation trade. Momentum is structurally prone to crowding. It is a purely price-based and self-referential signal. This makes momentum structurally negatively skewed (Figure 2). Gains are steady and gradual, but its crash episodes are disproportionately severe. This paper attempts to develop and test a set of crowding indicators drawing on cross-sectional price dynamics, options market information, fundamental valuation signals and trend analysis. The goal is to provide a structured framework for assessing when the risk/reward of holding momentum tilts unfavourably and, conversely, when a less crowded momentum factor presents a compelling entry point. records.text: We believe the sector is poised for a major oil capex upcycle, similar to that of the early 2000s, driven by five main factors: (1) Reserve life has contracted 25% since 2013 (proved FAS69 reserves), with Top Projects resource life down 65%; (2) Capex/boe is still c.40% below the peak, with exploration down c.60%; (3) Investors are starting to reward reinvestment and reserve life (c.20pp outperformance for high-capex companies over the past year); while (4) Reinvestment ratio is still c.15pp below the long-term average; and (5) The IEA has increased its 2030 oil demand forecast by 5 mnboed vs the 2021 NZE report, equivalent to the growth in China demand in the first decade of the 2000s. Finally, US shale production is flattening out, and all spare OPEC capacity is in the geopolitically challenging Strait of Hormuz. Oil services – especially deepwater – are well positioned, having consolidated with 2-6 major players per vertical (Seismic, OCTG, Drilling, Offshore) vs 6-15 a decade ago. In particular, we highlight Vallourec (premium OCTG) and TGS (seismic exploration) as key Buys exposed to this theme (16%/32% potential upside). records.text: GEMs Viewpoint | 19 April 2026 19 The current account deficit is expected at around 4% this year, broadly in line with our own forecast, before normalizing to about 3.3% over 2027 to 2031. Growth remains resilient at 4.4% in 2026, rising back to 5% during 2028 to 2031. FX reserves have decreased by over US$1.2bn since the beginning of the conflict reflecting external vulnerabilities. Inflation is expected to rebound to 6.5% by end 2026, increasing the probability that the central bank reverses its rate cutting cycle and hikes again. Zambia: Copper strength remains but the 2053s trigger uncertain The current account surplus is projected at 0.9% of GDP in 2026, rising to 2% in 2027 and 2028. This is a downgrade from the February report, which expected surpluses of 1.7% in 2026 and 2.6% in 2027. Zambia is one of the most exposed SSA countries to the conflict as oil accounts for 20% of imports. Nevertheless, a surge in energy and mining FDIs from 1.5% to 5% of GDP from 2025 to 2026 should support the Kwacha and limit the impact on the current account. The Bank of Zambia is expected to continue anchoring inflation on a downward trend, reflecting policy credibility and a commitment to price and FX stability. The government has reported spending close to US$200m in Q1 as foregone tax revenues to alleviate the impact of the oil shock. The baseline primary fiscal stance was expected to come in at around 1.5% of GDP so we expect these subsidies to bring it closer to primary break-even.

In other matters, as usual there was pessimism on the evolution of US and global imbalances from here and around geopolitical fragmentation. In the long run, experts tend to agree that there will eventually be a day of reckoning, but markets do not seem concerned for now and any decline in dollar dominance is expected to be gradual. On a cautious but relatively optimistic tone, experts noted that the direct impact of private credit on the financial system appears to be relatively small, and markets have generally proved resilient to shocks. This should provide some solace that financial stability risks do not appear imminent, but there are always concerns about financial interlinkages in the context of a relatively opaque market. The BoJ’s hawkish posture after the March meeting was likely conditional on viewing Middle East tensions primarily as a negative demand shock, without fully incorporating supply-side constraint effects such as supply-chain disruptions. However, feedback gathered from firms through the branch managers’ meeting was more cautious than initially expected. As a result, supply-side constraint factors, such as logistics disruptions, rising costs, and heightened uncertainty, appear to have been newly factored into policy discussions. From a policy discussion perspective, the implications differ materially depending on whether the impact of Middle East tensions is framed as solely a negative demand shock stemming from higher oil prices, or as a combination of a negative demand shock and a supply-side constraint shock. If viewed purely as a demand shock, higher oil prices would push inflation higher while restraining demand, potentially leaving the impact on underlying inflation broadly offsetting and preserving room for continued rate hikes. By contrast, if supply constraints are also taken into account, the resulting adverse effects on both inflation and growth would give rise to a more stagflationary dynamic, potentially making policymakers more cautious about further rate hik

records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 20 Apr 2026 04:28:14 ET │ 26 pages Global Economics & Strategy What We Learned in Washington DC CITI'S TAKE We summarize key takeaways from our meetings in DC, covering global markets and geopolitics, US, EU and other EM economies; namely, Brazil, China, Colombia, Egypt, Hungary, India, Indonesia, Israel, Mexico, Nigeria, Pakistan, Poland, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Turkey. Investors still cautious, but bullish EM overall; positioning suggest risk rally can continue. The highly uncertain near-term Middle East crisis cast a long shadow at the DC meetings, but the mood was far less somber than where we were in Spring last year after the Trump administration’s April 2, 2025 major tariff announcements. Overall, we thought most investors had been leaning on the bearish side with respect to (US) equities but have a bullish view on EM. However, given the heightened uncertainties of the Iran crisis, EM positioning still looks below underlying bullishness. The consensus from think-tank discussions on Iran seem to be that we are moving towards a negotiated solution. However, there was a sense that the situation could still escalate once more before it deescalates. A voice more closely aligned with the military argued that Iran has come to the negotiating table out of weakness and that the US has more leverage to push through the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz fairly soon.

The model The model we apply is a smooth-transition, local projections VAR, following the base methodology Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2011) and Tenreyro and Thwaites (2016). It allows for two states of the world (L and T in the equation below), each with different parameters informed by the data. The transition between these states is an estimated function of an exogenous variable (z). Each period in time is then a weighted-average of the two states, weighted by the transition function. For more on the model, see Appendix. yt+ ℎ = F (zt)(αℎ L + βℎ Lϵt + λLxt) + (1 − F (zt))(αℎ T + βℎ T ϵt + λT xt) + ut In our specific case, we include core CPI inflation, energy inflation, 3m/3m real GDP growth, inflation expectations and a measure of slack, captured by by the V/U gap estimated by Stelmach, Kensett and Schnattinger (2025), all at a monthly frequency. Our transition variable is the V/U rate, taking a high value when the labour market is tight, and a low value when the labour market is loose. As can be seen in Figure 1, the labour market was particularly tight in 2022 and is currently particularly loose. We estimate the model using local projections (Jorda and Taylor, 2025) and compute impulse responses based on the identified series of exogenous energy supply shocks provided by Baumeister and Hamilton (2019). This action followed a series of sustained global rate increases, persistent inflationary pressures, and a general environment of rising bond yields. The RBA's move signals a tightening monetary stance aimed at curbing inflation. Australian Bond Yield Sell-Off: Australian bond yields have experienced a notable "sell-off " – meaning bond prices have fallen, and yields have risen. This phenomenon has been driven by a confluence of factors: Middle East Conflict: Geopolitical tensions, particularly the conflict in the Middle East, often lead to increased uncertainty and can trigger a flight to safety in certain assets, but can also fuel inflationary expectations due to commodity price volatility, prompting central banks to maintain hawkish stances. Global Bond Yield Curve Bear Steepening: A "bear steepening" yield curve occurs when longer-term bond yields rise faster than, or while shorter-term yields fall or rise more slowly. This typically reflects market expectations of higher inflation and stronger economic growth in the future, or increasing term premium (investors demanding higher compensation for holding longer-duration bonds). records.text: 3. Is the market still pricing central bank policy too hawkishly? Yes, but the market opportunity is less clear than it was. We felt strongly that markets were overpricing the risk of hikes across a wide range of economies towards the end of March. At the point of maximum stress, options markets were pricing a high risk of large sequences of hikes not just from the ECB and BoE but also the Fed. As bonds have rallied, especially at the front-end of the yield curve, and volatility has declined, markets have moved closer to our policy views. For the US, market pricing is still clearly above both our baseline and scenario-weighted forecasts. The same is true to some degree in Europe and the UK. While this leaves us biased to look at front-end rate markets from the long side, the opportunities offer less asymmetry than they did. First, the gap between our forecasts and market pricing has narrowed. Second, the possibility of an extended period in which the Fed (and others) simply keep policy rates stable has clearly risen. Third, given the relaxation in pricing, any re-escalation of oil price risks has more scope to reignite fears about potential rate hikes than it did when multiple hikes were priced. Fourth, at the long end of global yield curves, we continue to think that rallies will be limited by fiscal pressures unless we see meaningful economic weakness. The back-to-normality scenario suggests that the RBA can once again focus on the cyclical side of the economy and not the structural supply induced stagflation risks. However, even under this scenario, our cash rate assumption remains unchanged compared to baseline. This is because a pick-up in consumer confidence, with already higher inflation, risks exacerbating inflation expectations and leading to a wage-price spiral with a tight labour market. This scenario could mimic some of the effects of 2022 where strong aggregate demand met supply-chain issues. The RBA would then be worried about inflation accelerating even further and may continue to hike policy rates. Consequently, we see terminal rate at 4.6%, implying two more hikes. But instead of back-to-back hikes, we see 25bp hikes across May and August instead, with risks still towards more. In this scenario, we would still expect the RBA to cut rates next year. Rates view. We would expect a more significant rally compared to baseline in this scenario. Bond yields would likely be around 10bps lower compared to baseline. However, in both baseline and upside scenario we expect higher rates, so therefore, duration would still be a better story for the second half of the year when the market can more clearly look to price policy cuts next for 2027. records.text: Australia Multi-Asset 20 April 2026 Citi Research 39 Scenario 2: Base Case–Moderate Pressure and Higher Inflation (US$112 Australian effective oil price, -0.4% GDP Growth, 1.2% CPI Inflation) This scenario introduces a more pressurized environment for the Australian real estate sector. Higher energy prices, a slightly deeper GDP contraction, and elevated CPI inflation collectively lead to increased challenges, primarily through higher finance costs. Finance Cost Impact: The impacts of higher bond yields and rising finance costs directly impinge upon earnings for real estate companies. This is particularly true for those with significant variable rate debt or needing to refinance at higher fixed rates. Increased debt service costs can compress net operating income (NOI) and reduce distributable earnings. Inflation Hedge for Certain Sectors: Crucially, the higher inflation in this scenario is best captured by sub-sectors with CPI-linked lease escalations, predominantly retail and industrial properties. These lease structures allow landlords to pass through a portion of the inflationary increases to tenants, thereby maintaining or even enhancing NOI. Discretionary Retail Resilience: Despite the broader economic pressures, discretionary retail real estate is expected to exhibit positive NOI growth. Still, as the labour market has continued to cool at the margin, weaker momentum in services CPI has started to materialise, as we argued in CEEMEA: Labour market key to squeeze out services CPI, dated 14 October 2025. January’s repricing in Hungary was also one of the most benign in decades, which we interpret as a signal that inflationary pressures are easing. Wage growth has been inflationary but this could change: Admittedly wage growth in Hungary has stabilised at higher levels compared to the pre-Covid decade, but we think compositional shifts have had an even greater impact on domestic inflationary pressures. Unit labour cost (ULC) growth has been the dominant contributor to sticky services inflation, a result of Fidesz’s policy of driving up wages through administrative measures (Figure 3). Higher investment could drive ULC lower: The stagnation in productivity has coincided with declining investment, as Hungary lost access to the majority of EU funds. We expect payout levels to remain high compared to history at >40% of CFO for EU Big Oils (vs 32% historically; peak at 120% in 2014) and >60% in the US (vs 45% historically; peak at c.100% in 2014). Structurally, US Oils have historically distributed a higher share of CFO to shareholders, while EU Oils have allocated more capital to investment, although this distinction has narrowed materially in the current cycle. Against this backdrop, reinvestment remains well below historical standards. During the quarter, AAPL launched the M4 iPad Air (March 2026), which should present tough comps with F2Q25, where AAPL launched both the M3 iPad Air and the 11th-gen base iPad. Offshore construction and EPCI: Since 2014, the offshore construction and EPCI industry has undergone a deep structural consolidation, which led to the number of Tier‑1 contractors capable of executing complex deepwater and SURF (Subsea, Umbilicals, Risers, and Flowlines) projects falling from 9 players to 7 today. The first phase focused on vertical integration, most notably the creation of TechnipFMC in 2017 through the merger of Technip and FMC Technologies, which established the first fully integrated subsea provider. This period also saw unsuccessful consolidation efforts and exits, including EMAS Chiyoda Subsea entering Chapter 11 in 2017 and the McDermott-CB&I combination in 2018. The second phase (2019-24) was marked by de‑leveraging and specialization: TechnipFMC spun off Technip Energies in 2021, while McDermott divested CB&I’s storage business in December 2024 for US$475m, leading to CB&I becoming a debt‑free standalone entity. The final super consolidation phase could occur in 2026 and reshape the competitive landscape. In July 2025, Saipem and Subsea 7 agreed to merge Saipem’s Offshore E&C business with Subsea 7; the acquisition is expected to close in 2H26 and would consolidate two of Europe’s largest offshore contractors into a single leading player. This is particularly true of the deeper downside tails: because the market has become more confident in a resolution path, developments that are large enough to shake that confidence are likely also to have meaningful market impact. We revisit the re-escalation scenarios we set out in late March and their impact across major assets. We consider two variants again, one in which oil prices move sharply higher again (we assume a somewhat more hawkish policy shock now given the relaxation we have seen since then) and one in which broad-based recessionary worries reappear. We find that the positions that offer the best leverage to the re-escalation scenarios in options markets come from downside in European assets, and in (US and European) credit and volatility indices. Oil itself is a clear beneficiary from re-escalation, so long positions in oil obviously protect against this risk. But implied volatility in oil options has fallen much less than for many other assets, so it offers less attractive leverage in options markets than these other assets. Deep downside in more classically cyclical assets like AUD and CAD also continue to screen well if a sharp re-escalation in the crisis leads to fear of a deeper slowdown. They may also provide protection against other downside growth risks (AI reversals, private credit, new shocks) that the market had worried about ahead of the Iran war. Angola: Cautious outlook but oil upside probably understated The macro outlook improves markedly on the back of higher oil prices. We are more optimistic than the Fund on Angola’s ability to benefit from the oil shock. In the absence of an IMF program, Angola’s recent agreement with the World Bank for a financing package of US$1.1bn positively anchors investor sentiment. The fiscal deficit is projected at 2.5% of GDP in 2026, improving from 4% in 2025, but then converging back to around 4% over 2027 to 2031. These projections appear conservative given the oil revenue uplift this year and the government’s stated consolidation ambitions. Gross government debt is expected to remain flat at 51% this year relative to 2025, then gradually decline by 1 to 2pp per year to around 57% by 2031. The current account surplus recovers to 2% this year but halves to 1% in 2027. We expect the CA surplus to outperform IMF’s expectations which could then translate into a combination of: a) higher FX reserves accumulation and/or b) faster reimbursement of Chinese oil-backed loans. This Time is Different (from 2022) — The Impact of Higher Energy Prices on European Manufacturing Industries The conflict in the Middle East and the near closure of the Strait of Hormuz (SoH) continue to cause large-scale disruptions to global energy supply. Energy prices have increased substantially since late February and our commodities analysts raised their forecasts significantly, expecting Brent oil at $83/bbl on average in 2026 (vs. $64/bbl before the conflict) and European natural gas (TTF) at EUR44/MWh (vs EUR34/MWh before). In this week’s Analyst, we analyse the implications of the energy price surge for European manufacturing industries, drawing on lessons from the 2022/23 European energy crisis and highlighting key differences between the current and the previous energy supply shocks. records.text: The industry response to the 2022/23 energy crisis was driven by four gas-intensive industries, which together accounted for about 70% of industrial gas consumption (Exhibit 5, right). In these industries, reduced gas consumption also led to lower production, although less than proportional to the reduction in gas consumption, indicating efficiency gains and production cuts in particularly gas-intensive goods. Aggregate industrial production stayed roughly flat, as output losses in gas-intensive industries—which accounted for about 18% of manufacturing output—were offset by gains in non-gas intensive industries. Leveraging a panel of sector-level industrial production across the major Euro Area economies, we find that supply-driven gas price shocks most negatively impact production in energy-intensive industries like basic metals or chemicals (Exhibit 6). While oil price shocks also weigh on energy-intensive industries, they affect manufacturing more broadly. Industrial production in capital goods producing industries, such as motor vehicles, machinery and equipment, computers & electronics, and electrical equipment, tends to decline notably after oil supply shocks. A key reason for the different impact is likely that gas markets are less globally integrated than oil markets, even less so in the past. Oil supply shocks thus tend to have more negative consequences for global demand. Accordingly, while the current shock is expected to be smaller and less persistent than the 202

Earlier, Tenaris consolidated the US shale OCTG market through the acquisition of TMK’s US assets (IPSCO) in 2020, which led to the removal of a key competitor in premium seamless. In parallel, Vallourec exited commodity markets and permanently closed high‑cost European mills, concentrating production in Brazil, the US and China, while TMK is now a regional CIS player following sanctions and the loss of Western premium market access. Industry structure has also tightened through “virtual consolidation” driven by trade policy and technology barriers. US steel tariffs (Section 232), raised to up to 50% on certain imports in 2025, have effectively regionalised the market, leading to foreign players localising capacity or exiting the market. As a result, OCTG has shifted from a volume‑driven global market to a premium, regionally protected structure dominated by vertically integrated producers. Pricing power increasingly rests on proprietary premium connections (TenarisHydril, VAM), now a prerequisite for complex US shale and deepwater wells, rather than tube capacity alone. The combined effects of M&A, capacity exits and trade protection have materially tightened the Tier‑1 landscape, reinforcing capital discipline and supporting structurally higher margins despite rig count cyclicality. records.text: Hong Kong IPO momentum has accelerated into 2026, with 40 listings ytd n raising US$14bn (+488% yoy), after reclaiming the top equity fund raising spot in 2025. The resurgence is underpinned by a shift towards “Hard Tech” and “New Economy” (Biotech, New Consumption), alongside a significant rise in A-to-H listings. Investor appetite remains robust, reflected by strong demand for new offerings and resilient post-IPO performance (+40% 1m post listing). A long queue of around 400 active applications underscores high issuer confidence. Our analysis of the HK market’s equity supply and demand indicates n sufficient capital for absorbing new issuances. For the full year 2026, we project a total equity supply of US$110bn, comprising US$60bn in new IPOs and US$50bn in post-IPO financing. This supply is expected to be met by US$180bn of corporate distributions (dividends and buybacks), US$20-30bn in capital reallocations from global long-term investors, and US$200bn in Southbound capital inflows, and continued strong active retail participation. HKEX continues to optimize its listing framework to facilitate new issuances, n notably shortening review timelines, and allowing confidential filing for technology enterprises. records.text: PM summary With OPEC global spare capacity running down, US shale reaching maturity and reserve life eroded by underinvestment, we were already seeing signs of a new oil capex cycle, similar to that of the early 2000s. The escalation of geopolitical tensions in the Middle East since February 28 may have accelerated the timing of a structural capex upcycle, which we now expect to start in 2027 (see: Falling oil reserve life points to M&A and long-term price upside), driven by the following: The industry needs to re-invest in reserve life with more exploration capex: Oil reserve life from major developments is down 65% since peak, mirrored by a 25% decline in proved reserve life, as the industry has been focused on short-cycle and brownfield to support lower decline rates in the near term at the expense of longer reserve life. Conventional discoveries have remained low, with Oil & Gas capex/boe still c.40% below the peak and exploration down c.60%, tilting the sources of new reserves increasingly toward revisions and M&A rather than organic exploration-led additions. As a result, our Top Projects cost curve has continued to steepen since 2017, with higher breakeven underscoring the need for a meaningful step-up in exploration spend to replenish the inventory of projects. records.text: Market structure in offshore services has materially improved The oil services industry has been structurally transformed over the past decade, shifting from being a highly competitive, fragmented market with frequent new entrants to a tightly consolidated industry characterised by high barriers to entry and a limited number of global players. Offshore drilling: Since 2014, the offshore drilling industry has undergone a structural consolidation with the number of key offshore drillers falling from 15 players to 8 today (‑60%), driven by a decade‑long cycle of bankruptcies, mergers and asset transfers. Between 2016 and 2021, Valaris, Seadrill, Noble, Diamond Offshore and Pacific Drilling all filed for Chapter 11, which led to fleet rationalisation. The consolidation phase accelerated post restructuring: Transocean acquired Songa Offshore (2018) and Ocean Rig; Noble absorbed Pacific Drilling (2021), Maersk Drilling (2022) and Diamond Offshore (2024); Seadrill acquired Aquadrill (2023); ADES acquired Shelf Drilling (2025); and Transocean expects the closing of the Valaris acquisition in 2H26. As a result, modern high‑spec fleets are now concentrated among a handful of operators that control the majority of seventh‑gen drillships, harsh‑environment floaters and premium jack‑ups. Media reports indicate that Fed Chair nominee Kevin Warsh’s Senate Banking Committee confirmation hearing will be held on 21 April. Judging from Treasury Secretary Bessent's comments this week, we expect Warsh’s testimony to favour an on-hold, wait-and- see posture for monetary policy over the short run. In the medium term, we expect Warsh to express some optimism that rate cuts could eventually resume. All in all, we think the market could read these comments as somewhat dovish to market pricing, supporting the 2s30s steepening view. Furthermore, even if Warsh does not reveal a near term rate policy bias, he could reiterate his big picture views – arguing for a smaller Fed Balance sheet, and “redeploying” it in the form of lower rates – which strongly supports a steepening bias in Treasuries. In contrast to our call for steeper curves in both EUR and USD, we think in Japan the risk–reward is attractive to position for 5s10s IRS to flatten. Czechia: strong starting point, restrictive rates, and focus on core inflation Overall, the tone was one of vigilance rather than urgency: policy rates are viewed as appropriately restrictive for now, with decisions to remain firmly data and forecast driven. The Czech economy was described as entering the current energy price shock from a position of strength, having started with inflation below target, restrictive interest rates, and robust growth. While higher oil prices are expected to have some impact (mainly via prices rather than shortages), the overall effect on GDP is seen as limited, with growth remaining above 2% across scenarios. The koruna’s strength has been a welcome development, reinforcing disinflationary forces, while food prices are contributing to easing headline pressures. Monetary policy remains firmly focused on core inflation, which should stay around 3%, a level consistent with maintaining a tight stance but not, on its own, a trigger for further tightening. Policymakers repeatedly stressed that Czechia’s situation differs from the euro area: ECB hikes would affect model trajectories but do not mechanically require a response, as domestic policy is already restrictive. records.text: What could a revival of the IPO market mean for private equity? The number of global private equity deals has risen steadily since the Global Financial Crisis, fueled by historically low financing costs. By 2025, total AUM across private strategies have surpassed US$15tn. Despite this global growth, China’s share in international portfolios has contracted over the past five years due to geopolitical tensions, regulatory shifts, and a pronounced home bias among developed-market investors. In response, domestic Chinese PE firms and state-owned capital have aggressively stepped in, acquiring strategic assets and sustaining the momentum of private investment. A prolonged period of subdued equity performance and stagnant IPO activity created a significant “exit backlog” for PE and venture capital (VC) funds during 2023–2024. However, the revival of the Hong Kong IPO activities in 2025-2026 has proved to be a pivotal catalyst, and effectively reopened the exit window for backers previously constrained by the stringent listing requirements of mainland A-share markets and the regulatory complexities of US listings. The ability to access public markets in Hong Kong has mitigated the liquidity crunch, triggering a re-acceleration of Chinese private equity investment since mid-2025. records.text: Australia Multi-Asset 20 April 2026 Citi Research 38 Real Estate & Property Real estate stands as a fundamentally capital-intensive industry, heavily reliant on debt financing for acquisitions, development, and operational activities. Moreover, property valuations are subject to dynamic changes as capitalization rates (cap rates) adjust over time, reflecting shifts in investor sentiment, perceived risk, and market fundamentals. A critical mitigating factor, however, is the positive correlation between higher inflation and properties with Consumer Price Index (CPI) linked leases, providing a natural hedge against rising costs for certain asset classes. He was explicitly empirical, sceptical of mechanical Taylor -style rules (while accepting their benchmark value). The message: watch the data, pursue the dual mandate, and avoid over - tightening based on fragile estimates of r -star. He also raised financial-stability and balance-sheet risks earlier than predecessors. Overall, his stance preserved consensus: evolve the framework, don’t break it. Warsh’s hearing yesterday was the opposite —explicitly disruptive. While stressing Fed independence, he criticised the Powell-era Fed and called for regime change and a new inflation framework. On policy tools, he reiterated his critique of balance -sheet ex pansion, favoured rate -based policy, and floated unspecified “new tools”. On communications, he would not commit to post -meeting press conferences, arguing the Fed overcommunicates —a sharp reversal from the Bernanke-to-Powell push for transparency. On inflation, he signalled a move away from hard numerical rules, describing price stability as an inflation rate “not talked about”, and endorsed broader gauges —citing a forerunner of PriceStats/the billion prices project—and a preference for median measures over core PCE. US Administration Portrays Strength The US administration suggests that growth is strong, and expects consumption to hold in well given rising real incomes and a resilient labor market. Given a much lower breakeven level for NFP (around 50k or lower) the economy is likely to continue to generate enough jobs to support the consumer. AI productivity gains is expected to continue, which suggests Fed hikes won’t be necessary. The oil shock is seen as concerning, but inflation will likely be narrowly focused on energy and short-lived. With respect to tariffs, the view is that tariffs based on Section 301 will be used to mostly replicate the tariff agreements that were reached with other nations. The relationship with China is in a good place and there is no desire to escalate on this front. In other words, we think we are seeing a shift in the nature of US-China – one of “strategic rivalry” towards “strategic accommodation” . Australia faces a structurally higher effective oil cost compared to Brent oil because of its heavy reliance on Asian refiners, which are highly exposed to SoH supply chains. This systematically incorporates higher Singapore refining margins, Asian OSP premiums as well as incrementally higher freight and insurance costs. In other words, Australian imports have paid a premium to the spot oil prices. Generally, this premium has been low and manageable, particularly during times of stability. However, given the current crisis is not just a price shock but a physical supply shock, the premium is higher than historic averages. Consequently, we believe the baseline scenario should be an “effective oil price” , that is a premium to our Global commodity analysts forecast. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

Against this backdrop of heightened interest, this report details the views of European investors on the three main themes that were central to our conversations. Theme 1: Growing skepticism of a BoJ April hike — The black box of the reaction function Many investors expressed skepticism about an additional rate hike at the April meeting. The immediate cause for this is a situational judgment that the BoJ will be reluctant to act amid uncertainties like significant geopolitical risks and an unclear outlook for fiscal policy. Underlying this caution, however, is a more fundamental frustration that the BoJ's policy reaction function itself remains difficult to understand. Investors repeatedly asked, "Ultimately, which economic and financial indicators does the BoJ prioritize?" However, while the consensus is for the BoJ to remain on hold, a sense of tension was also present, with some noting that "we won't know until the last minute," suggesting the final decision is unpredictable. n Policy dilemma : Given current domestic inflation trends and the accelerating depreciation of the yen, there was a strong normative opinion that the BoJ "should raise rates." records.text: Lack of exploration spending and success continues to drain resources 2004-16 saw two Oil & Gas ‘revolutions’ fuelled by cheap financing, leading to industry fragmentation and a compounded 10% cost inflation over that period. The first Oil & Gas revolution (2004-13) was driven by national oil companies that deployed their rising free cash flow into rapid international expansion with a combination of exploration and M&A activities. At the same time, market perceptions of long-term supply shortages incentivized independent Oil & Gas players to step up their ambitions and become operators of major developments across the globe. The second Oil & Gas revolution (2009-16) was led by US Exploration & Production companies, unlocking 100+ bn barrels of US shale oil resources. Post Covid, conventional oil discoveries have remained weak and few additions were made to our Top Projects reserve base. In 2025, we added three material discoveries to our database, Bumerangue (Brazil), PEL 85 (Namibia) and the Omega Alfa exploration campaign in Norway. For Bumerangue, BP’s largest discovery in 25 years, we currently assume close to 2bn boe of estimated reserves in place. It brings our total Top Projects oil conventional additions to c.2.5bn in 2025, which tracks above 2024. records.text: Review of 2025-26 IPOs Hong Kong’s IPO market reclaimed its position as the world’s top fundraising venue in 2025, with 119 new companies listed raising approximately US$36bn. The momentum has accelerated into 2026, with 40 listings raising US$14bn year-to-date. The resurgent Hong Kong IPO activities are driven by a structural shift toward “Hard Tech” and A to H listings, accounting for 25% and 53% of total funds raised since 2025. AI, Robotics and Biotech firms saw overwhelming retail and institutional demand and strong post-IPO performance. Certain foreign favorite A-share listed companies have issued H shares even on price premiums (to their A-share tickers), reflecting strong interest from international investors in Chinese equities. Demand for new IPOs and post-IPO performance remain strong (+40% 1m post listing) in 2025 and 2026 year-to-date. Notable trends include: 1) A-to-H listings continue to dominate the deal calendar year-to-date, with 15 A-share companies listing in HK in 1Q26; 2) The new listings are concentrated in Hard Tech (Semiconductors, AI, Robotics) and Biotech (Chapter 18A), supported with favorable listing rules (see Section 4). 24 out of 40 new listings are AI-related and Health Care companies; and, 3) We note increasing involvement from global long-term capital acting as cornerstone investors. The current supply shock driven by high oil prices happens after the BCCh has missed the inflation target three times over the past five years. Under these conditions, policymakers may have lower tolerance to “look through” the current shock as this could risk missing the target for at least another year, jeopardizing the bank’s credibility. records.text: M Update 2 March CPI Bank of Canada Implications The composition of the March CPI print is unlikely to materially shift the Bank of Canada’s near-term policy assessment. The core measures remain contained and, importantly, there is little evidence so far of a sustained broadening in underlying price pressures. Recent communications from Governor Macklem and the tone of the Governing Council’s March deliberations emphasized the need to see clearer signs of more generalized pass-through before reassessing the current stance. Against that backdrop, we expect the Bank to retain its view at the upcoming meeting that policy is at an appropriate level for now, while continuing to monitor if incoming data show any change in inflation dynamics. Inflation Dynamics The Bank of Canada’s preferred core measures were flat on a 12-month basis, and contained on a 3-month basis. Both CPI Trim and CPI Median were roughly flat, with CPI- Median at 2.3% and CPI-Trim at 2.2% (down from 2.3%). While both accelerated on a one- month and three-month basis, they were coming from extremely low levels, closer to 1% than 2%, and this increase was likely a reversion toward target, and not a beginning of a strengthening trend. Headline driven higher by energy prices: Headline CPI rose 2.4%Y in March, accelerating from 1.8%Y in February and reversing the prior month’s base-effect-driven softness. records.text: The conflict in the Middle East and the near closure of the Strait of Hormuz (SoH) n continue to cause large-scale disruptions to global energy supply with meaningful increases in energy prices over the last month and a notable upward revision to our energy price forecasts. In this week’s Analyst, we discuss the implications of the energy shock across European manufacturing industries, highlighting three key differences vs the 2022/23 European energy crisis. First, the current price shock is expected to be smaller and less persistent, while n the decoupling from Russian pipeline gas that began in 2022/23 has been sustained. Accordingly, we expect the aggregate impact of the shock to be smaller, and capacity shutdowns in energy-intensive industries should be less likely than during the 2022/23 crisis. We estimate a 2% hit to industrial production by the end of 2027, which compares to our previous estimate of a 4% hit to industrial production from the 2022/23 crisis. Second, the current supply shock is less gas-centric and more oil-driven. The n 2022/23 crisis was fundamentally driven by a sharp reduction in Russian pipeline gas supply to Europe and impacted a narrow set of highly gas-intensive industries particularly hard. The current shock is primarily an oil supply one that tends to reduce industrial production more broadly while also impacting capital goods producers and export-oriented sectors negatively. records.text: m Chinese authorities to smooth RMB appreciation. The People's Bank of China (PBoC) has shown an upward bias in its daily fixing, indicating a preference to slow the RMB’s appreciation pace. PBoC bias on FX reappears: Previously, with a steady USD and the RMB index well above 100, there was less pressure when the PBoC delivered a higher fixing. However, the PBoC posted a fixing 392pips above market estimates (Figure 1) on 15 April, pushing the RMB index below 100. We think this strongly indicates that the PBoC prefers to smooth the downward move in USDRMB spot – especially as China still faces criticism over its rising current-account surplus. We still see room for the index to consolidate further and for the USDRMB spot to stabilize, as the last time the PBoC adopted a defensive stance to the RMB basket was when the index fell below 97. The risk is that a further USD sell-off driving the USDRMB spot below 6.80 could prompt additional exporter-driven USD sales, recreating the February episode when the fixing’s upward bias failed to curb appreciation expectations and market positioning. That said, if the PBoC’s commitment to FX stability remains unchanged, it may once again step in with measures to temper excessive appreciation, just as it did in February (see China FX: PBoC shows support to curb excessive one-way RMB appreciation, dated 27 February). records.text: Services: Expect in-line revenue growth, slight App Store acceleration We estimate Apple F2Q26E Services revenue of ~$30.4 bn (+14% yoy), in line with Apple’s prior guidance for Services revenue to grow in line with overall F2025 Services revenue growth (+14% yoy). The two largest contributors to Services revenue should be App Store (~24% of Services revenue, F2Q26E revenue +7% yoy GSe) and TAC (~22% of total Services revenue, +12% yoy), which along with strong DD% yoy growth across Apple’s other Services categories, should support Apple in achieving its guide. As we will discuss later in our App Store analysis, we continue to believe App Store should be a meaningful driver of Services revenue over the long run despite concerns around third party payments. That said, we expect near-term App Store revenue slowness (<9% yoy growth) and investor concerns to persist through F1Q27E driven by (a) competition from off-app payment options; (b) headwinds from changes in commission fee structures in China and Japan; (c) threat of App Store disintermediation from vibe coding apps (though we believe Apple is appropriately addressing this risk via App Store policy enforcement); and (d) macro-economic volatility. However, we expect continued faster growth across Apple’s broader Services categories to support >10% yoy Services revenue growth through the rest of F2026E. There are several trends underpinning our expectations for Apple to be able to maintain >10% yoy quarterly Services revenue

The two components are then summed into a single composite implied skewness score, which is percentile-ranked over its history. The options market is in many ways a more forward- looking crowding gauge than price-based measures. Residual correlations reflect what has already happened in positioning while implied skewness signals what options traders expect to happen. When crowding is building, that expectation tends to manifest in the volatility surface before it shows up in realised returns. The two indicators are therefore complementary. Decile Analysis The decile analysis for the implied skewness indicator (Figure 6) uses a one-month lag, reflecting the more forward-looking nature of options pricing. The pattern that emerges is directionally consistent with the price-based results, but the signal structure differs in an important way. Key Takeaways Rather than being concentrated in a single extreme decile, the deterioration in forward momentum returns begins earlier. The four indicators developed in this paper are designed precisely to address this limitation, each capturing a distinct facet of the crowding cycle and operating at a different point on the signal horizon spectrum. The price-based crowdedness indicator and the average implied skew are reactive signals. Both are designed to flag crowding as it builds – and to clear quickly when positioning normalises. They are the early warning layer of the scorecard. The valuation spread, by contrast, is a slow-moving, fundamentals-anchored signal.
