records.text: US Rates Weekly 19 April 2026 Citi Research 10 drained and instead was allocated to funding markets, eventually pushing repo rates significantly higher. We have long argued that the funding stress last year was driven by increased collateral, rather than due to reserves being scarce. Indeed, the XCCY basis, such as SOFR/TONAR, tightened as repo rates in the US moved higher. Since December, repo rates have normalized once again due to a combination of factors: the Fed’s RMPs which dampened the seasonal collapse in reserves, smaller T-bill auction sizes which reduced the total outstanding T-bills and collateral funding needs, along with a reduction in the balance of the TGA into mid-April. Furthermore, the uncapping of the SRP (formerly SRF) back in December also likely helped support year-end liquidity. We are lightly updating our T-bill issuance forecasts for the rest of the year (more on this below) and see a risk that issuance could surprise on the upside in the second half of 2026. However, even if this risk scenario materializes, we think the XCCY basis will likely remain resilient as it did last year. An outstanding question is if the Fed will aim to actively smooth reserves seasonality the rest of the year. On monetary policy, we do not expect a change in the 40% effective funding rate at the upcoming MPC meeting, but the decision between holding the one week repo rate at 37% with funding at the upper band, or hiking the repo rate to 40%, remains finely balanced. Capital Inflows: We anticipate a recommencement of global interest and capital flows into the Australian real estate sector. This is often driven by investors seeking stable, long-term returns in a low-inflation, relatively low-interest-rate environment, where real assets offer a compelling value proposition. Increased liquidity and demand from foreign investors can underpin property values and transaction volumes. Leasing Dynamics: While lower inflation implies a reduced pass-through benefit from CPI-linked leases, this scenario is conducive to supportive domestic consumer demand. Strong consumer sentiment and spending are expected to translate into positive leasing spreads for the retail and industrial sectors. Retailers benefit from increased foot traffic and sales, while industrial properties gain from robust e-commerce activity and supply chain demand. These are notable revisions from our 2026-27 Outlook when long 30y gilts was one of our Top Trades for this year from our optimism on UK inflation, low volatility, expectations of quieter politics, a weaker labour market and lower duration supply. The risks to our forecasts are to the downside in a scenario where we see a permanent ceasefire and the re-opening of the Strait of Hormuz, which would bring down breakeven inflation component of yields. Markets appear to have interpreted this as meaning that, given the elevated uncertainty, the BoJ is likely to stay on hold at the April meeting for now. records.text: 4. With no peace deal yet in sight, isn’t it clearly premature to price this kind of relief? We don’t think that it is clearly premature, especially for forward-looking equity markets, but it does leave markets vulnerable to any meaningful challenges to a resolution path. We have encountered a lot of skepticism that the current relief is justified, given that there is still plenty of room for negotiations to break down in ways that renew the upward pressure on commodity prices and generate more visible signs of shortages and rationing. We have argued that this kind of disconnect is not uncommon during relief from crises. For equity markets in particular, the bulk of asset relief comes when the market feels comfortable reducing weight on the deep tails, not when the worst of the economic reality is being felt. As in corrections driven by monetary policy tightening, the market may feel comfortable looking beyond upcoming economic weakness if the main source of the pressure appears to have peaked, even if the worst of the economic impact has not been felt. We do not think it is inherently surprising that the market has reacted to incomplete but positive steps towards a resolution that it was even less confident about ahead of time. If the market can maintain its confidence that a resolution is coming, even meaningful delays to the resumption of oil flows, and the possibility of larger shortages and economic disruptions, may not have a sustained impact on equity pricing. records.text: Michael Metcalfe 22 April 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General The Warsh Fed: less talk , less guidance, but a billion prices Every Fed Chair confirmation hearing is a negotiation between a nominee and the Senate over one fundamental question: how much discretion will you exercise, and against what framework? They are not, in themselves, a policy statement, but they do signal how Fed policymaking will evolve and yesterday’s signalled a transformation Greenspan’s 1987 hearing set the template: strategically opaque, anti -inflation, and unwilling to define a numerical target. Rate guidance was largely absent—the message was simply: trust me. It worked while credibility held, but it substituted personality for framework clarity. Bernanke’s 2005 hearing was a reaction: he openly backed inflation targeting—rules-adjacent, expectations -anchoring and transparent. That approach, reinforced by his research on the Depression and Japan’s lost decade, laid the groundwork for forward guidance and eventually QE. Eight years and a financial crisis later, Yellen’s hearing emphasised the dual mandate and how the Fed would exit extraordinary accommodation, gradually. It leaned on thresholds—unemployment below 6.5% and inflation forecasts above 2.5% for one to two years (the Evans rule)— a rules-like communication strategy for cautious discretion. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 622/04/2026 Intuition & Rationale Our fourth indicator approaches crowding from a complementary angle, measuring the extent to which the momentum factor’s price level has deviated from its own recent trend. The intuition is straightforward: when a factor becomes crowded, capital inflows push its price above its fundamental trajectory, generating a detectable departure from trend. Construction Methodology We compute this deviation using a rolling approach. At each date, we fit a linear trend over the preceding three years of the BNPFMOM1 Index and define the crowding score as the percentage deviation of the current price from this rolling trend. The score is then percentile- ranked over its history to produce a 0-100 reading. Decile Analysis The decile analysis (see Figure 9) reveals a clear and monotonic relationship between the deviation score and subsequent one-month momentum returns. Across the lower deciles, average returns are positive, reaching approximately +1% to +1.4% in the least crowded bucket. As the score rises, returns decline steadily and turn negative from around the 60th percentile onward. Key Takeaways This pattern is consistent with the price-based and implied skew indicators and confirms that an elevated deviation from trend is a meaningful signal of crowding risk. records.text: Australia Multi-Asset 20 April 2026 Citi Research 45 Reasons for the Negative Relationship: Cost of Capital: Rising bond yields translate directly into a higher cost of debt for REITs, as their financing costs for both new projects and refinancing existing loans increase. This higher cost of capital can compress profit margins and reduce distributable earnings. Discount Rates: Investors typically use bond yields (or a spread over them) as a component of the discount rate when valuing future cash flows from real estate assets. As bond yields rise, the discount rate applied to REITs' future earnings increases, leading to lower present valuations. Alternative Investment Appeal ("Bond Proxy"): REITs are often viewed as "bond proxies" due to their relatively stable income streams (rents). When bond yields are low, the dividend yields of REITs appear more attractive. However, when bond yields rise, they offer a more competitive, low-risk income stream, reducing the relative appeal of REITs and potentially diverting capital away from the sector. Capitalization Rates (Cap Rates): While not identical, cap rates often correlate with bond yields. As the risk-free rate (proxied by bond yields) increases, investors typically demand higher cap rates for real estate investments, which directly translates to lower property valuations if net operating income remains constant. records.text: Australia Multi-Asset 20 April 2026 Citi Research 43 Fund Flows into Specific Sectors: Continued strong fund flows into defensive and growth-oriented sectors like convenience retail and industrial properties are expected. Investor demand in these segments remains robust due to their perceived stability and growth prospects, helping to maintain compressed cap rates. Net Operating Income (NOI) Growth: Crucially, net operating income growth, particularly from the inflation pass-through mechanisms embedded in CPI-linked leases, will serve as a vital counterbalance. In retail and industrial assets, where CPI-linked leases are prevalent, rising inflation can translate directly into higher rental income. This increased income stream can help to maintain or even boost property valuations, offsetting the dilutive effect of higher funding costs on cap rates. In summary, while the broader environment of higher funding costs will exert pressure on real estate cap rates and valuations, sectors with strong underlying demand (industrial, convenience retail) and those with effective inflation hedges (CPI-linked leases) are better positioned to mitigate these impacts through sustained income growth and continued investor interest. This creates a nuanced landscape where careful sector selection becomes paramount for investors. Figure 54. Cap rates © 2026 Citigroup Inc. No redistribution without Citigroup’s written permission. records.text: Australia Multi-Asset 20 April 2026 Citi Research 8 The effective oil price – the base case for Australia We establish an effective oil price of US$112/bbl for the Australian economy throughout 2026. This reflects the premiums that Australian importers must pay. This price target reflects a market that is beginning to price not only benchmark risk, but the rising cost of securing physical barrels. While the Brent oil price could sit anywhere between US$85-$95/bbl, the effective price is arguably $15-$25 higher. During global supply shocks, the economic impact is often determined less by the quoted Brent price and more by the delivered cost refiners must pay to source prompt cargoes. As inventories tighten, refiners may need to bid materially above benchmark levels for available barrels, lifting feedstock costs across the system. Therefore, even if some disrupted flows are eventually restored and the headline geopolitical risk premium moderates, tighter inventories, elevated freight costs, and stronger physical differentials could keep the effective cost to the economy above the benchmark price Examining the different scenarios. T o gauge the impact of various oil price scenarios, we run scenarios for Australia's effective oil prices. nScenario 1 (base case) – The effective price at US$112/bbl: This assumes that Australian importers will continue to pay a premium above the spot price for Brent. records.text: Australia Multi-Asset 20 April 2026 Citi Research 19 The impact of the US-Iran conflict on AUD will be a function of: 1.T o what degree global financial conditions tighten and weigh on risk assets (the “macro”). 2.How the RBA chooses to respond to the stagflationary shock vis-à-vis current market pricing and other central banks like RBNZ (the “micro”). We think the former will be the primary driver of G10 FX and, in our base case, supports AUDUSD downside over Q2. But given the RBA/RBNZ views of Citi Economics, the latter presents relative value opportunities to buy AUDNZD dips. Global macro: stagflation headwinds? The first lens of our analysis relies on how the global macro backdrop evolves in coming months. Our base case has remained stagflationary risks look underpriced and a backdrop of tighter global financial conditions is USD-positive (Global FX Strategy - Risk/reward attractive for USD longs). If such a backdrop materializes, it would impact AUD as a crowded long among investors and as a currency that historically exhibits a high beta to global growth expectations. Citi Global Economics downgraded global growth in their latest monthly forecast update. The lack of conviction in any particular view of the impacts on the Brazilian economy at this time was stressed by BCB last week. Nonetheless, we think Brazil's strategic decision from several years ago to pursue pre-salt oil licensing has proven prescient, transforming the country into a net oil exporter and providing a critical buffer against the current energy price squeeze. Thus, while the government has deployed approximately USD 2bn in subsidies to mitigate the impact on diesel and refined products, a portion of these costs has been offset by higher net oil export revenues, limiting the fiscal drag. This energy self-sufficiency distinguishes Brazil from regional peers. On the fiscal outlook if the Lula administration were to win the polls (now a very close fight), fiscal policy discussions are centering on mandatory expenditures, particularly the need to reform the BPC (Benefício de Prestação Continuada—a monthly cash transfer to low-income elderly and disabled individuals that requires no prior social security contributions). records.text: US Rates Weekly 19 April 2026 Citi Research 16 USTs: Officials moved into T-bills Data on foreign holdings of USTs (TIC) for the month of February showed that demand for long-term USTs slowed down after a strong start to the year in January. Overall, foreign holdings of long-term USTs decreased by $8.5bn on a value- adjusted basis (Figure 29). The decrease was mainly driven by foreign officials whose long-term UST holdings decreased by about $33.9bn (z-score of -1). However, we do not think this decline was due to outright sales of USTs. Foreign officials seemed to have moved some of their long-term UST holdings into T-bills. On the other hand, foreign private investors purchased about $25bn of long-term USTs (z-score of 0.1). Overall, in the first two months of the year, foreign investors purchased $48.9bn of long-term USTs, in line with what we saw in the first two months of 2025 ($51.1bn). T-bill holdings of foreign investors increased by $91.6bn in February (z-score of 3). That was the biggest month of foreign T-bill purchases since April 2020. As we mentioned earlier, this was mainly driven by foreign officials who sold some of their long-term UST holdings and purchased 67.8bn T-bills. Foreign private investors also purchased about $23.8bn T-bills. On a market value basis, the Treasury reported a net increase of $106bn in foreign UST holdings. Tariff levels declined steadily in recent months, falling to 8.5% in February, with the decline accelerating after the Supreme Court ruling. The decision on IEEPA forced a shift in underlying tariff authorities, with country-level IEEPA tariffs temporarily reconstituted under Section 122. We have long argued (even before any 2025 tariffs) that the legal basis for durable tariffs would need to be anchored in section-based authorities rather than IEEPA. Current Section 122 tariffs expire on July 24, 2026. After that, we expect more durable authorities such as Sections 301 and 232. Typically, new-issue 5y TIPS auctions in April have always seen very strong demand from both foreign investors and domestic investment funds. This led to April TIPS auctions consistently clearing through the when-issued levels over the last decade (Figure 25). However, the April TIPS auction in 2025 tailed by almost 2bps. This was most likely because, the growth outlook was bleak heading into that auction after the Liberation Day tariff announcements in the first week of April (Figure 26). Yet another one of these stories is the appropriate way to measure legal services prices in PCE. PCE legal service prices have typically corresponded with legal services prices in CPI inflation. However, it was a surprise for many forecasters when a substantial 11% increase in estimated legal services in January CPI did not boost PCE inflation in January. Instead, legal services in PCE seemed to correspond much more closely with legal services prices in PPI data. In the press release for February PCE, the BEA noted the adjustment made to January legal services calculations1. But February PCE legal services did not have a similar adjustment and again better aligned with CPI. It is unclear what measure (PPI or CPI) will correspond to March PCE legal services. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W keep page margin clear keep page margin clear keep page gutter clear 222/04/2026 A crowding scorecard Sources: BNP Paribas A framework that relies on a single indicator will be either too slow to warn or too noisy to act on. The four indicators in this paper address this limitation, each capturing a distinct facet of the crowding cycle and operating at a different point on the signal horizon. The price-based crowdedness indicator and the average implied skew are reactive signals. Both flag crowding as it builds and clear quickly when positioning normalizes. They form the early-warning layer of the scorecard. The valuation spread, by contrast, is a slow-moving, fundamentals-anchored signal. It does not react to short-term positioning flows; it accumulates over months and years as persistent inflows structurally reprice the long leg relative to the short leg. It is the memory of the scorecard. The deviation from 3-years trend sits between the two, providing a macro-level read on whether the factor as a whole has overshot its structural trajectory – a useful cross-check that contextualizes the other signals within the broader factor return cycle. The current scorecard configuration shows why this multi-dimensional approach is needed. Price-based and implied skew indicators are at low percentiles, suggesting momentum is not acutely crowded today. With calculated industry-level output per employment in hand from 1Q 2006 through 4Q 2025, we then assign each a measures of AI exposure using the criterion in Felten et. al. (2021). 1 . The authors identify occupational exposures to AI and weight those occupations across NAICS 4-digit industry categories. From there, we grouped various industries into three categories: top-25% AI exposure, middle-50% AI exposure, and lowest-25% AI exposure. In total, we compute output per employment in 64 industries, with 12 industries with high exposure to AI and 26 industries with low exposure to AI. The remaining 26 industries are classified as having medium AI exposure. We then compare and contrast the evolution of output per employee. The industry output data we use for our output measures are published once a quarter in the third GDP release; the industry employment data are published monthly in the Employment Situation. records.text: xpected to serve as significant catalysts for investment attention. Historically, US mega-IPOs could divert global capital away from secondary n markets, occasionally triggering short-term “crowding out” effects. Conversely, these landmark listings often exert positive spillover effects on the valuation and performance of sector peers in China. Our analysis of US IPOs exceeding US$1bn over the past two decades reveals a distinct pattern in Chinese equity performance around these events. We find that the MSCI China Index typically performs softly in the week preceding a large US listing; however, Chinese stocks in the same sector tend to outperform in the subsequent week. This post-listing momentum suggests that investor focus often shifts toward broader industry developments and fundamental synergies between domestic firms and their newly listed global peers. records.text: ing real incomes, keeping inflation containment central. The external position is still manageable despite an expected CA deficit of around -3.7% of GDP in 2026, and up to -5.0% by 2028. Higher oil prices provide upside risk to these projections. Trade patterns are also adjusting structurally, with the share of Russia in overall trade having declined significantly. Oil exports are seen as stable at around 98-99Mt this year and up to 105 Mt in 2027, still mainly through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium route, with alternative routes as a backup. Inflation is assessed to be in the high single digit to low double digit range, justifying a continued emphasis on macro stability. Monetary policy is firmly restrictive, with the policy rate at 18% and the authorities stressing strict data dependence. High real rates, together with higher reserve requirements to absorb excess liquidity, reinforce this restraint. While surveys suggest potential for around 200bp of easing over time, this is conditional on sustained disinflation. A stronger exchange rate is expected to aid the disinflation process through negative FX pass through, supporting a gradual normalization path. Fiscal policy structurally benefitted from VAT reform. The authorities reported a substantial increase – around 50% – in VAT revenues, driven both by higher compliance and a broader tax base, with further gains expected as new taxpayers are fully incorporated. The inflationary impact of VAT changes is estimated at 1.5-2.5

It does not react to short-term positioning flows; it accumulates over months and years as persistent inflows structurally reprice the long leg of the factor relative to the short leg. It is the memory of the scorecard. The deviation from long-term trend sits between the two, providing a macro-level read on whether the factor as a whole has overshot its structural trajectory – a useful cross-check that contextualises the other signals within the broader factor return cycle. The current configuration of the scorecard illustrates precisely why this multi-dimensional approach is necessary. The price-based and implied skew indicators are both at low percentiles, suggesting that momentum is not acutely crowded today. Yet the valuation spread remains at historically elevated levels – a legacy of the exceptional momentum run of recent years that has not yet fully mean-reverted. This is not a contradiction; it is a description of where we are in the crowding cycle. The trade has been de-crowded from a positioning standpoint, but the fundamental premium embedded in the long leg has not unwound. The risk is therefore not immediate – but it is latent. Should momentum attract renewed inflows in the current environment, the starting valuation level means the crowding cycle could re-intensify faster and from a higher base than historical precedent would suggest. records.text: Preview of IPO Pipeline The Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) currently oversees a pipeline of approximately 400 disclosed IPO applications, excluding confidential filings. Among the +400 companies, 59 of which are seeking listings under specialized regimes tailored for “pre-revenue” biotech firms (Chapter 18A) and “Specialist Technology” enterprises (Chapter 18C). Furthermore, the pipeline includes 53 overseas-incorporated Chinese entities, i.e. Red-Chips and P-Chips, and 104 companies that are already listed on the A-share market. The backlog underscores strong issuer confidence and reinforces Hong Kong’s status as the leading global fundraising hub for Chinese companies. The current IPO backlog is predominantly concentrated in the Information n Technology and Healthcare sectors, accounting for 62% of all applications. Enterprises capable of delivering unique value propositions are strategically positioned to capture significant investor attention and capital inflows. We anticipate that investor preference will remain focused on outperforming segments—specifically Artificial Intelligence (AI), biotechnology, and new consumption—as these areas continue to drive innovation and growth. Premier A-share companies with strong international appeal are increasingly n leveraging H-share fund-raising to tap into recovering global investor demand. records.text: GEMs Viewpoint | 19 April 2026 5 Europe Ruben Segura -Cayuela BofA Europe (Madrid) Struggling to find the upside As it is often the case during IMF meetings and the Small Talks conference there was a general perception that Europe was in a very delicate situation. A year ago, the mood was better with hopes of a faster push for defence, a full agenda of reforms, the German fiscal package, and the hope that the, back then, new Franco-German relationship could lead the region into a brighter medium-term outlook. This has changed. The energy price shock comes on top of the lack of substantial progress on reforms, a trade war, and a sustained policy uncertainty shock. Yes, there is an important move in defence, but that will take years to allow the region to break current dependences. And even in Germany, despite recent policy initiatives, the general view was one of scepticism things can get much better and, in line with our view, a general sense that fiscal, by now, will be useful to avoid a proper recession but not enough to reshape the German economy. If anything, the periphery, particularly Spain, seems to be the main perceived bright spot across speakers and investors. On cyclical developments, most investors agreed with our view on the economy. The energy price shock is another challenge that will likely bring the economy almost to a halt for a few quarters despite the deployment of the ambitious German fiscal package. records.text: Thesis summary, rating, price target, key risks We are Buy rated on Apple with a 12-month target price of $330 (unchanged) reflecting 34X (unchanged) our NTM+1Y EPS. Key risks include: Weakening consumer demand for products and services. Apple’s products and services are typically sold to consumers and any weakness in the macroeconomic environment could reduce demand for Apple products and services. Apple generated ~50% of its revenue from iPhones (F2025), which is highly dependent on purchases driven by upgrades. Lengthening replacement cycles due to macroeconomic headwinds, improved product durability, or lackluster product innovation could all negatively impact upgrade demand. Supply chain disruption. Although Apple’s suppliers have a global footprint, the majority of final assembly occurs in China. Increased geopolitical tension may result in disruptions to global trade including through tariffs. While Apple has a robust supply chain network, it may rely on one or a few key suppliers for unique or hard-to-manufacture at scale parts. Intensifying competition. Apple competes across personal devices (e.g., handsets, tablets, PCs, headphones) and a variety of services (e.g., video streaming, app distribution, advertising, music streaming, online fitness, cloud storage, product warranties). records.text: The industry needs to re-invest in reserve life A decade of energy under-investment has cut the Oil & Gas industry’s proved reserve life by c.25% since 2013 According to SEC reported reserve data, the industry’s proved reserve life remains on a downward trend at 10.2 years in 2024, c.25% lower than the 2013 peak and well below the 30-year average of 12.3 years. Reserve life peaked at a 30-year high of 13.3 years in 2013 before entering a structural decline driven by under-investment after 2014. Oil reserve life was at 10.0 years in 2024 (down vs 9.8 years in 2023 and 13.0 years in 2013), broadly flat in recent years following the decline post 2013. Gas reserve life was at 10.6 years in 2024 (vs 10.7 years in 2023 and 13.7 years in 2013), with a more gradual decline over the past decade. As outlined in our Top Projects report, under-investment in oil, an increasing focus on returns, de-leveraging, free cash flow, and operational efficiency and ongoing capital discipline have taken a toll on oil resource life. According to our analysis, the resource life of Top Projects (recoverable resources/production) has more than halved in 2026, from 55 years in 2012 to 19 years, a 65% decrease over the past decade, painting a tougher long-term supply picture. records.text: DEEP DIVE D E E P D I V E KEY MESSAGES Momentum has been one of the best-performing equity factors over recent years – but the more crowded a trade becomes, the more violent the unwind. Here we present a four-indicator scorecard for the US momentum factor. It combines price dynamics, options market signals, fundamental valuation and trend analysis, each capturing a different stage of the crowding cycle. Residual return co-movement and implied skew, the positioning-based indicators, are below alert thresholds, suggesting the momentum trade is not currently crowded. However, fundamental indicators tell a different story. While the valuation spread between momentum winners and losers is still below its crowding threshold, it is getting closer to it. The deviation form trend is just above its threshold, flagging a crowded environment. Overall, momentum remains an attractive trade for now, though caution is warranted – the tools below will help you monitor crowding and identify optimal exit signals. 22/04/2026 1 Chloe Duban, Cross-Asset & Macro Quant Strategist | BNP Paribas London Branch. Please refer to the end of the document for important information and MAR disclosures. There doesn’t seem to be any plans to pursue unconventional monetary policy measures or to inject liquidity via government bond purchases. Instead, Bo T seems to prefer channeling liquidity injections through the banks to improve credit intermediation. Rate hikes would only be considered if inflation expectations become unanchored, but they don’t see evidence of this yet. Any fiscal support on the back of the Iran crisis will likely remain limited, focusing more on targeted income support, rather than trying to cap retail fuel prices through excise tax cuts/fuel subsidies. If the Iran crisis drags on for longer than expected and economic conditions deteriorate, fiscal policy will likely be seen as being needed to take lead on the policy response, and not monetary policy, with the possibility of an emergency decree to increase borrowing capacity. In such an emergency, threat of a ratings downgrade (Thailand has a negative action from S&P and Fitch) may not be a sufficient deterrent. In other words, it seems the bar for more aggressive fiscal policy seems lower than for additional monetary easing if growth outcomes worsen. records.text: M Foundation 6 Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 show the evolution of our estimates of labor productivity growth in industries with low-, medium-, and high-exposure to AI based on our BEA and BLS industry-level inputs. The exhibit plots the four quarter percentage change in estimated labor productivity. In 2025, output per employee was rising the fastest and accelerating the most among the industries Morgan Stanley Research has identified as the high AI exposure industries. Productivity growth in industries with closer to the median exposure had a sideways trend. Productivity in industries with the lowest exposure fell slightly. Between 2011-2019, labor productivity growth in industries with high AI exposure averaged 1.1% per year. In 2024 and 2025, this accelerated to 2.1% and 5.7%, respectively. By way of comparison, productivity growth for industries with medium exposure to AI accelerated to 1.4% per year in 2024-25, from 0.5% in the decade leading up to the COVID pandemic. Finally, productivity growth in low-AI exposure industries improved modestly, rising by 0.7% per year in 2024 and 2025 after falling 0.1% per year between 2011-19. The main driver of higher labor productivity is faster output growth, not labor displacement As we noted in the introduction to this report, AI has created both optimism and anxiety; optimism about faster productivity and output growth and pessimism about the risks for labor replacement. We see a mismatch between the current low hiking premium and clear upside risks for inflation in a context of Chile’s central bank missing the target band over the past five years. We now expect the BCCh to hike the policy rate by 50bp to 5% in 2026. Even if the Middle East ceasefire holds, we think inflation risks will ease less than the downside risks to activity. We favor a spread payer against SOFR to cushion the risk of oil prices and global yields falling sharply and suddenly if positive developments in Middle East peace negotiations surprise the market. LLC Global Markets Comment: Beyond Relief—A Cross-Asset View 19 April 2026 | 10:04PM EDT Markets have seen substantial relief as the ceasefire and negotiation process n have progressed and oil prices have dropped, with US equities and some other assets already at fresh highs. We revisit our cross-asset frameworks here to answer the questions we are encountering about what might come next. The cross-asset pattern since late March is broadly consistent with what we n would expect from a “relief” scenario based on a fall in oil prices and some reversal of growth and policy fears. But that relief has come with less of a fall in oil prices and in interest rates, so oil prices and bond yields are still clearly higher than they were before the war began. US growth pricing is close to our baseline forecast already, though the market has unwound less of the initial hawkish policy shock. We think it is more common than skeptics might think for relief to occur largely n on the reduction of deep tail risks. So long as the market can maintain its conviction that a resolution is likely in the coming months, near-term economic damage and setbacks—even material ones—may not have a large impact on equities and other longer-duration assets. TURKEY- A Pending “Tweak” to Monetary Policy Turkish policymakers are navigating a challenging backdrop characterized by decelerating domestic demand and elevated energy-driven inflation risks. The oil shock is expected to drive high inflation in April to May with widespread prices increases across energy/transportation, food and core goods, though service disinflation looks intact amid economic slowdown. Against this backdrop, meeting CBT’s year-end inflation target in the “low 20s” will likely be challenging (Citi f ’cast: 29.7%). Revisions to the inflation forecast are expected to be communicated in May, once the duration of the conflict can be better assessed. Though Turkey went into this Iran crisis with already moderating activity (e.g. 0,4% QoQ real GDP growth, softening labor markets, negative auto sales growth, slowing card spending and retail sales) and relatively contained CAD (a far better position than where they were in 2022), the Iran crisis could weigh on disinflation expectations. records.text: Early indicators point to a much less asymmetric shock this time. Producer prices for basic chemicals have started to increase meaningfully in China and petrochemicals prices in China and Europe have risen to a similar degree over the past month (Exhibit 8). The loss in competitiveness resulted in a decline in net exports, by about half in nominal terms in 2022 and as a share of GDP (Exhibit 9, left). This was driven by a particularly strong increase in imports in the most energy-intensive industries (Exhibit 9, right). This surge in imports, on the one hand, intensified competition in energy-intensive industries and weighed on production. On the other hand, lower-cost imports from countries less affected by energy price increases helped reduce cost pressures for industries that use energy-intensive intermediates as inputs. In principle, there is a bit more scope to unwind the hawkish policy shock since the war began, but without a sharper fall in oil prices, we think scope for further policy relief may also be more modest now. A larger drop in oil prices on a more permanent reopening of the Strait, and a further drop in implied volatility in oil markets (which is still elevated relative to many other assets), would be more obvious sources of further relief. Looking at versions of further relief scenarios, including one with a clearer fall in oil prices and another with less of an oil price decline, we find that modest growth and policy relief would in most respects resemble a smaller version of what we have seen so far. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 3 Industries with high AI exposure are seeing labor productivity from faster output growth, not labor replacement In our effort to better understand AI and US economic transformation, we published a report that examined lessons learned from prior innovation waves (see Lessons from the five innovation waves that preceded AI, 6 April 2026), where we concluded that history suggests AI, like prior general purpose technologies, can be expected to increase productivity; create temporary labor displacement during the transition phase, but not permanent employment losses; lead to a boom-bust cycle; put further pressure on income and wealth inequality; and alter how education is provided. First up: AI and labor markets We then put history to the test, first by investigating to what degree AI adoption is causing dislocations in the US labor market (see AI Labor disruption: More micro than macro so far, 6 April 2026). We found that occupational data, when grouped according to AI exposure, point to early, narrow AI displacement — most visible among younger workers — while aggregate disruption remains small at about 0.1pp on the unemployment rate. We also found signs of overall task reshuffling. We plan on using this analysis as an ongoing tracker of AI diffusion and labor market disruption. records.text: indicates the long leg trades at a historically elevated premium relative to the short leg, beyond normal cross-sectional valuation dispersion. The link to crowding is intuitive and grounded in literature. Momentum baskets are long recent winners and short recent losers. Normally, winners trade at a moderate premium – a valuation gap reflecting genuine earnings momentum and compensated by forward returns. When the trade becomes crowded, persistent inflows push winners' valuations higher, detached from fundamental improvement. The spread widens not because the longs are better businesses, but because too much capital chases the same stocks. This dynamic precedes momentum crashes: the long leg becomes expensive, the short leg cheap, and potential energy for a sharp mean-reversion builds. This indicator is the only one anchored in fundamentals, not market microstructure or options pricing. Decile Analysis Using a six-month lag, the decile analysis matches the slow-moving nature of fundamental valuation signals. The results are compelling and, crucially, easier to interpret than at shorter horizons. In the lower six deciles, returns are broadly positive, showing that only the tail of the valuation distribution carries the warning signal. For REITs, a steeper yield curve implies higher borrowing costs for long-term projects and potentially higher discount rates applied to future cash flows. Stronger-Than-Expected Domestic Economic Conditions: Robust economic data, including resilient Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth, low unemployment rates, and persistent inflationary pressures, have strengthened the case for higher interest rates. A strong economy, while generally positive for corporate earnings, can also signal that inflation is entrenched, leading bond investors to demand higher yields to compensate for the erosion of purchasing power. The Negative Relationship Between A-REITs and Bond Yields Historically, REITs have often exhibited characteristics similar to bonds, particularly their income-generating nature. Consequently, their performance tends to be inversely related to bond yields. Strong Negative Relationship: As observed in the analysis of monthly data between 2022 and 2026 (excluding periods of extreme volatility like the Global Financial Crisis and the initial phases of the COVID-19 pandemic), most Australian REITs (A-REITs) demonstrate a strong negative relationship with 10-year Australian Treasury yields. This means that when 10-year bond yields rise, A-REIT performance (specifically, their "excess return over the ASX200") tends to decline, and vice-versa.
